# Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability

Jiaming Wang Affiliation: Meituan
Email: [wangjiaming15@meituan.com](mailto:)    Yunke Zhao
Affiliation: Meituan    Peng Ding    Jun Kuang Affiliation: Meituan   
Yibin Shen Affiliation: Meituan    Zhe Tang Affiliation: Meituan   
Yilin Jin    Zongyu Wang Affiliation: Meituan    Xiaoyu Li
Affiliation: Meituan    Xuezhi Cao Affiliation: Meituan    Xunliang Cai
Affiliation: Meituan

###### Abstract

The capability to precisely adhere to instructions is a cornerstone for
Large Language Models (LLMs) to function as dependable agents in
real-world scenarios. However, confronted with complex prompts, LLMs
frequently encounter difficulties in fulfilling all specified
requirements within a single response. Drawing inspiration from recent
advancements in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and self-correction
methodologies, we introduce Meeseeks¹¹ 1 The name is inspired by Mr.
Meeseeks from “Rick and Morty,” a character renowned for efficiently
accomplishing assigned tasks. See:
[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Meeseeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Meeseeks),
a fully automated iterative instruction-following benchmark equipped
with an integrated feedback mechanism. Meeseeks identifies erroneous
components in model responses and provides corresponding feedback
accurately, thereby iteratively guiding the model toward
self-correction. The dataset contains over 700 curated instances
annotated by 32 distinct capability tags in Chinese and English.
Extensive experimental results reveal that different state-of-the-art
commercial and open-source LLMs exhibit vastly disparate performance,
and even after 20 turns of iterative feedback-driven self-correction,
nearly all models demonstrate suboptimal performance. We conducted
comprehensive analysis and uncovered numerous common issues prevalent in
current state-of-the-art models, as well as several counterintuitive
phenomena. Meeseeks has been open-sourced on
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Meeseeks-156A](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Meeseeks-156A).

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents have become essential tools in various applications, from
customer service to content creation ([Minaee et al., 2025](#bib.bib28);
[Wulf and Meierhofer, 2024](#bib.bib46); [Pandya and Holia,
2023](#bib.bib32); [Lee et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Qian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib33)). However, as their use expands, the instructions
users provide are often complex and multifaceted, posing challenges for
accurate execution ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib31); [Zeng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib51); [Stolfo et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Hou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14); [Zhao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib55); [Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib52)). Instruction following, or the ability to execute
tasks based on natural language commands accurately, is critical for
LLMs to be reliable in real-world scenarios. For instance, in
healthcare, an LLM might need to generate reports with specific word
counts or mention key terms multiple times. Misinterpreting such
instructions could lead to errors with serious consequences ([Li et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib25); [Qiu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib36)). Similarly, in
finance, precise adherence to instructions ensures compliance and
accuracy, avoiding potential risks ([Arun et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Kim
et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). These content creation tasks require LLMs to
have strong text instruction-following capability. To evaluate the
instruction-following ability of today’s LLMs, researchers employ
instruction-following benchmarks to determine how effectively LLMs can
align with human intentions. This research indicates that models are
unable to address problems flawlessly in scenarios where prompts contain
numerous constraints.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been primarily developed to enhance
the reasoning capabilities of LLMs in mathematical and logical tasks by
guiding them to generate intermediate steps ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib44); [Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib43); [Yu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib50); [Zhang et al., 2022](#bib.bib53)). Building upon CoT,
self-correction techniques enable LLMs to identify and rectify errors in
their reasoning processes.  ([Kumar et al., 2024](#bib.bib20); [Huang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Liu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib26); [Ganguli
et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Liu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib27)). While
existing self-correction methods are primarily evaluated on mathematical
or logical problems, we extend this approach to multi-constraint
instruction-following tasks to probe the upper limits of LLMs’
instruction-following capabilities.

Therefore, we introduce Meeseeks, a multi-turn automatic
instruction-following benchmark with feedback system. The framework
enables Meeseeks to fully automatically identify specific constraints
that the LLM fails to meet and explicitly explain the reasons for such
failures. The system operates in successive rounds, where Meeseeks
evaluates the LLM response, provides feedback, and then assesses the
resulting self-correction. Moreover, Meeseeks applies a more challenging
dataset embedding 32 capability tags and 3 cognitive evaluation
dimensions (intent recognition, granular content validation and output
structure validation), examining the entire thought process of the model
to establish an integrated instruction-following ability evaluation
system. Furthermore, due to the high cost of single to multiple turns
evaluation and more challenging data, Meeseeks introduces a code-guided,
rule-augmented LLM-based evaluation to reduce cost and raise accuracy of
the evaluation workflow. Meeseeks reveals nuanced patterns in LLMs’
multi-turn self-correction abilities that challenge conventional
understanding of instruction following as well as a significant gap
between different LLMs’ single-attempt instruction-following performance
and their upper-limit instruction-following capability. Even after 20
rounds of self-correction, all prevailing LLMs still fail to provide
responses that satisfy all constraints. In conclusion, our main
contributions are:

- •
  We introduce Meeseeks, a challenging multi-turn automatic
  instruction-following benchmark that operates in successive
  evaluation-feedback-correction cycles across 32 capability tags and 3
  evaluation dimensions. The framework accurately identifies constraint
  violations, provides targeted feedback, and evaluates LLMs’
  self-correction attempts.
- •
  We present an enhanced automatic evaluation pipeline by introducing a
  novel code-guided, rule-augmented LLM-based evaluation framework.
  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method
  significantly outperforms existing approaches, delivering substantial
  improvements in evaluation accuracy, raising accuracy from 78.7% to
  98.4%.
- •
  We conduct experiments across 17 state-of-the-art models and observe
  that despite implementing 20 iterations of feedback-driven
  self-correction mechanisms, both leading commercial and open-source
  LLMs consistently failed to achieve accuracy rates exceeding 91%.
  Through systematic analysis, we identify both common and distinct
  limitations among these models, thereby contributing valuable insights
  and establishing reference benchmarks for future model development and
  optimization efforts.

## 2 Related Works

IF-Eval ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib56)) pioneered comprehensive
instruction-following evaluation by introducing rule-verifiable
instructions (e.g., “Include keyword1, keyword2 in your response”).
While this approach enables automatic verification, the dataset’s
simplicity and synthetic nature limit its applicability to real-world
scenarios. Subsequent benchmarks, such as InFoBench ([Qin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)), CELLO ([He et al., 2024a](#bib.bib11)),
FollowBench ([Jiang et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), and COLLIE ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib49)), advanced the field by employing constraint-based
frameworks to handle more complex data. However, these methods still
rely on specific format constraints for evaluation. Complexbench ([Wen
et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)) effectively addresses these limitations by
leveraging rule-augmented, LLM-based evaluation processes. This approach
eliminates the need for extensive prompt restrictions, allowing for more
flexible response formats from the evaluated LLMs. Current
instruction-following benchmarks are predominantly designed for
single-turn interactions and fail to capture the complexity of
multi-turn conversational scenarios, thereby limiting their
effectiveness in comprehensively evaluating models’
instruction-following capabilities. Parrot ([Sun et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39)) introduced a framework for collecting human-like
multi-turn instructions that mimic natural dialogue patterns.
Multi-IF ([He et al., 2024b](#bib.bib12)) extended IF-Eval to multi-turn
sequences across multiple languages, revealing performance degradation
in later turns and in non-Latin scripts. StructFlowBench ([Li et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22)) proposed a structured framework with six types of
inter-turn relationships to evaluate dialogue coherence and contextual
understanding. However, these multi-turn benchmarks typically allow LLMs
only a single attempt at each turn, introducing new requirements in
subsequent turns. In contrast, Meeseeks allows models self-correct their
response as the turn iterates.

## 3 Meeseeks

Meeseeks implements an iterative self-correction framework comprising
response collection, evaluation, and feedback prompting
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
More specifically, given questions with multiple constraints, each
iteration follows three steps: (1) collecting responses from the model
while enforcing all constraints, (2) evaluating the response against
each constraint, and (3) providing constraint-specific evaluation
results and explanations as feedback to prompt the model for
self-correction in the subsequent iteration. The following sections
provide a comprehensive overview of Meeseeks.
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evaluation ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
and
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Feedback Prompting ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
provide details of evaluation and feedback prompting respectively;
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
explains our code-guided, rule-augmented, LLM-based evaluation
addressing cost and accuracy challenges in multi-turn frameworks,
serving the evaluation;
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Data collection, Taxonomy and Quality ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
presents the quality control and the structure of our dataset;
Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Metrics ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
elaborates on metrics used in our experiments.

### 3.1 Evaluation

Due to hallucinations in LLM, directly relying on them to determine
whether each constraint is satisfied by the tested model’s response is
unreliable ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Li et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib23); [Zhu et al., 2024](#bib.bib57); [Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9); [Qiu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib35); [Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Hao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Bang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Yan et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)). Therefore, our
primary method for judging constraints consists of two steps: first, use
an LLM evaluator to format the model’s response (typically by converting
it into a Python list); second, employ a Python script to assess whether
each constraint is correctly satisfied. To facilitate the format
section, the framework integrates a dual format mechanism: the coding
format, which activates the code-specific pipeline when coding flags are
present (flag detail:
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Data Structure ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability");
coding format detail:
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")),
and the regenerate format, which formats model responses through
regeneration. The evaluation procedure is bifurcated according to the
rule labels associated with each constraint. For constraints with null
rule labels (see
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Data Structure ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")),
the LLM evaluator assesses the response directly, without any
formatting. When specific rule labels are present, corresponding
rule-based Python judgment scripts are invoked to verify the validity of
the formatted content.

### 3.2 Feedback Prompting

After evaluation, each constraint is accompanied by a judgment
explanation; if a constraint is unmet, the feedback specifies the reason
for failure. With the exception of a small portion of feedback generated
directly by the LLM evaluator, the majority of feedback is automatically
produced by the constraint-specific scripts. These evaluation results
and corresponding feedback are integrated into the tested LLM’s chat
template for subsequent turns, serving as targeted guidance for its
self-correction. The framework monitors improvement after each
self-correction iteration.

### 3.3 Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation

Addressing the limitations of rule-verifiable instructions and format
constraints problem mentioned in Section
[2](#S2 "2 Related Works ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability"),
the prevailing method is to employ an LLM-based approach to eliminate
redundant prompt constraints. This approach identifies and retains core
content by eliminating auxiliary text, followed by rule-based evaluation
to ensure compliance with specific constraints. Consider the Prompt:
Write me a research report about LLM, make sure the report should
include less than 2000 words, and the example problem shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability").

|                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $`\circ`$ Raw Model Response                                                                         |
| Response: Okay, I will write you a 2000-word essay. LLM is…(1998 words). I hope you like the answer. |
| Check: Word count: 2014 \> 2000 $`\rightarrow`$ Constraints unmet \[INCORRECT\]                      |
| $`\circ`$ Formatted Model Response                                                                   |
| Response: Okay, I will write you a 2000-word essay. LLM is…(1998 words) I hope you like the answer.  |
| Check: Word count: 1998 \< 2000 $`\rightarrow`$ Constraints met \[CORRECT\]                          |

Table 1: Raw model responses can introduce evaluation errors during
Python script execution. The prevailing method regenerates the model
response and cleans the redundant texts.

However, this approach encounters significant challenges in both
computational efficiency and accuracy. For long model responses (such as
extended essays) and large-scale multi-element generation, the LLM-based
format extraction requires regenerating entire clean texts to remove
non-essential components, resulting in substantial computational
overhead. Furthermore, format accuracy degrades considerably as the
complexity of model responses increases, creating a scalability
bottleneck for practical applications. To address these issues, we
propose a code-guided, rule-augmented LLM-based evaluation.
Specifically, we use prompts to guide the LLM to format model response
by coding, rather than having the model regenerate all context. By
applying the function created by the LLM Evaluator, the necessary
information can be formatted efficiently without the regeneration step
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.4 Data collection, Taxonomy and Quality ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
Through experimental validation, we demonstrate that our code-guided
formatting delivers substantial improvements in evaluation accuracy with
performance gains reaching 97.46%, while achieving up to 71.08%
reduction in token consumption compared to prevailing formatting
approaches (See
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experiments on Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).

### 3.4 Data collection, Taxonomy and Quality

Meeseeks comprises over 700 meticulously curated instances in Chinese
and English, annotated with 32 distinct capability tags, and with a
substantially greater difficulty compared to existing datasets in the
domain. The dataset is collected from our business log and rigorously
formatted to templates
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Sample Data Parameterized Template ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")),
wherein all constraints are manually annotated by professional
annotators to ensure both precision and contextual relevance. Similar to
prevailing instruction following benchmarks, the prompts from our log
also contain multiple output constraints, and we use a
cognitive-inspired framework that decomposes instruction-following into
three fundamental dimensions
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Meeseeks ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")):
Intent Recognition, Granular Content Validation, and Output Structure
Validation. This framework employs hierarchical capability tags across 3
levels and 32 capability tags in total, with lower levels subordinate to
higher ones
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Capability Tags ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
Data instances are systematically generated by varying template
parameters and synchronously updating the associated constraint
variables, with NO involvement of LLM at any stage of data generation.
To further enhance the reliability and objectivity of the evaluation,
all subjective capability constraints—such as those assessing emotional
intelligence in model responses—are deliberately excluded from the
dataset. For quality assurance, we recruit three experienced annotators,
each holding at least a bachelor’s degree with professional expertise in
data annotation, and conducted comprehensive reviews of every data
instance and its associated constraints, rigorously verifying their
validity and consistency. For instance, they identified and resolved
logical contradictions, such as cases where one constraint required the
inclusion of an "idea" while another simultaneously prohibited a "great
idea," thereby ensuring the integrity and coherence of the synthesized
data.

Table 2: Our code-guided, rule-based evaluation instructs LLMs to
generate code for formatting model response, thereby replacing the
regeneration techniques employed in existing methodologies.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation accuracy on Meeseeks’ own dataset.
We have our annotators independently assess responses generated by
Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4o-20241120, and DeepSeek-R1. Given the
straightforward nature of the evaluation tasks for human assessors, we
are confident in the annotators’ ability to provide accurate evaluations
of the LLM responses. Following the collection of evaluation results, we
analyze inter-annotator agreement and observed over 99% consensus among
the three annotators, demonstrating strong reliability in our human
evaluation framework. Any remaining discrepancies were manually reviewed
to ensure final quality assurance. Through this rigorous evaluation
process, we achieve a substantial improvement in end-to-end accuracy
from 78.7% (The prevailing format accuracy on the Meeseeks dataset) to
98.4%.

### 3.5 Metrics

Serving as trustworthy agents, LLMs must fulfill all requirements
specified in the user’s prompt for the responses to be considered
usable. Utility rate reflects the ratio of usable responses to total
evaluated responses and is essential for evaluating an LLM’s
effectiveness as a practical and professional agent. Additionally, to
help researchers identify subtle differences in instruction-following
abilities between different LLMs, we propose the Meeseeks score, which
indicates the overall capability tag accuracy of the LLM (see formula in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Metric ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
Furthermore, Meeseeks generates a capability report with accuracy
statistics across various capability levels, enabling researchers to
understand the instruction-following proficiency of LLMs from different
perspectives (sample report in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Sample Capability Report ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
The accuracy metric denotes the utility rate hereafter.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experiments on Code-guided, Rule-augmented LLM-based Evaluation

To evaluate the effectiveness of our code-guided, rule-based evaluation,
we conduct experiments in two distinct scenarios: long single element
generation, where the model is tasked with producing a complete article,
and large-scale multi-element response generation, where the model is
required to generate a substantial number of comments (These two
frequently used scenarios are utilized and modified from Complexbench’s
dataset). For long single element scenarios, we choose the question: A
man is performing on stage for the audience, … Please continue and
expand this passage with at least 20 sentences. We vary the required
number of sentences from 0 to 500 with an increment of 1, generating
synthetic data. For large-scale multi-element scenarios, we choose the
question: People are … Please write an essay. Requirements:
Argumentative essay, objective and neutral language style, no less than
800 characters. Similarly, we set the required character count from 50
to 5000 (in increments of 100, and rather than use "less than", output
length is required in a certain range), generating synthetic data and
answers. The ratio of correct to incorrect answers in both scenarios is
set to 1:1, and employed Qwen2.5-32B + Qwen2.5-32B-Coder  ([Qwen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib37)) as the evaluator (also for main experiments).
Subsequently, we conduct a comparative analysis of the accuracy and
token consumption patterns exhibited by the code-guided and prevailing
formatting methods
(Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1 Performance Gap On First and Last Turn ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).

In large-scale multi-element scenarios, the code-guided formatting
approach exhibited substantial performance gains over the prevailing
method. It attained an average end-to-end accuracy of 0.994 with an
average token usage of 252.94, compared to the prevailing formatting’s
accuracy of 0.684 and token usage of 874.65—yielding a 45.32%
improvement in accuracy and a 71.08% reduction in token consumption. In
scenarios with long single element, code-guided formatting sustained
high efficacy, achieving an end-to-end accuracy of 0.998 and average
token usage of 98.73, whereas the prevailing approach encountered severe
hallucinations and often misidentified core content, resulting in an
accuracy drop to the baseline level of 0.5 and token usage of 191.99;
this translated to a 97.46% accuracy enhancement for code-guided
formatting. The limitations of prevailing formatting primarily arose
from its token-saving strategy, which defaulted to outputting merely the
"thinking process" and "ALL" without supplementary context ("ALL"
indicates that the evaluator considers the model’s response to be free
of redundancy). Efforts to address this by employing advanced evaluators
such as GPT-4o yielded no discernible benefits, suggesting that the
underlying issue resides in the few-shot prompt architecture of the
prevailing method. These outcomes highlight the enhanced robustness and
resource efficiency of code-guided formatting in varied and demanding
contexts.

### 4.2 Main Experiments

We evaluate 17 representative LLMs over 20 turns and find models from
commercial APIs consistently demonstrate superior performance in both
single-turn and multi-turn dialogue settings (When the input length
surpasses the maximum context window capacity of the evaluated LLM, the
instance is automatically classified as failed). Notably, o3-mini (high)
achieves the highest performance from turn 1 through turn 5. In
subsequent turns, Claude Sonnet 4 Thinking surpasses other models,
establishing itself as the best-performing system in extended
interactions. However, despite 20 turns of feedback-guided
self-correction, the performance of most models remained suboptimal. In
the following sections, we provide a systematic interpretation of the
phenomena presented in
Table [3](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability").

## 5 Analysis

### 5.1 Performance Gap On First and Last Turn

We design the experiment such that models were only required to correct
questions they had previously answered incorrectly in subsequent turns.
Theoretically, as the pool of questions that can be answered correctly
diminishes, the performance gap between different models should
gradually narrow. However, our findings indicate the opposite: the
disparity between models actually widens with an increasing number of
turns. Through this iterative process of correction over multiple turns,
we can progressively approach the upper limit of a model’s
instruction-following capability. This phenomenon suggests that the
difference in the upper limits of instruction-following abilities among
various models is substantially greater than the single-turn performance
differences might suggest
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
Concurrently, we observe that the rankings of the models evolve across
turns, and their correlation with the initial ranking in the first turn
progressively weakens. We calculate the Pearson and Spearman correlation
coefficients between the model rankings in Turn 1 and those in each
subsequent turn. The results reveal that the correlation between a
model’s performance in a single attempt and its upper limit of
instruction-following ability initially diminishes rapidly and
subsequently plateaus as the number of turns increases
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
This further reinforces our earlier conclusion: the disparity between a
model’s single-turn instruction-following performance and its ultimate
capability ceiling is more significant than initially anticipated.

Figure 2: Our code-guided formatting demonstrates remarkably consistent
performance in both token utilization and accuracy metrics.

### 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags

To further elucidate the underlying reasons for suboptimal model
performance, we examine the identified issues through the lens of
constraint satisfaction. Specifically, we analyze these challenges from
the perspective of our three top-level capability tags along with some
additional findings.

Figure 3: As the turns iterate, the standard deviation of utility rates
gradually increases; The correlation between subsequent round rankings
and turn 1 rankings shows a declining trend.

Output Structure Validation When models are tasked with generating
multiple contexts (e.g., producing numerous titles or names), their
outputs exhibit substantial redundancy, with minimal improvement
following feedback interventions. Despite explicit feedback indicating
which content elements are duplicated, virtually all evaluated models
demonstrate limited capacity to rectify such extensive redundancy issues
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
In more demanding scenarios, when models are required to generate
content adhering to specific proportional constraints—for instance,
producing 20 pieces of copy with a long-form to short-form ratio of
3:2—we observe that most models fail to accurately determine the
requisite quantities of long-form versus short-form content. However,
reasoning contents in reasoning models help predetermine the quantities
of long and short content within their reasoning processes, thereby
mitigating such failures.

![Refer to caption](2504.21625v6/capabilitytagsnew.png)

Figure 4: Performance trends varied significantly across models and
capability tags.

Granular Content Validation Within this dimension, model deficiencies
are predominantly concentrated on word count accuracy. We observe that
models fundamentally lack precise word counting capabilities; however,
they should theoretically possess a general awareness of output length
([Hiraoka and Okazaki, 2024](#bib.bib13); [Zhao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib54); [Kaplan et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Vieira et al.,
2025](#bib.bib42)). Indeed, our experiment shows that models would
adjust their output length to align with specified requirements through
our feedback mechanism
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
Nevertheless, we identify a critical phenomenon: when models receive
feedback indicating that their output word count fails to meet
requirements—accompanied by the actual word count—they frequently
exhibit severe overcorrection behaviors. For instance, when the
requirement specifies approximately 400 words (with acceptance criteria
of 360-440 words), and the model’s initial output contains 300 words,
upon receiving feedback regarding the word count deficiency, most models
initially make modest upward adjustments (e.g., to 330 words). However,
upon receiving subsequent feedback indicating continued insufficiency,
catastrophic overcorrection occurs: outputs may abruptly escalate to 600
words. This adjustment momentum exhibits bidirectional persistence, with
subsequent iterations potentially plummeting to 100 words. While we
observe that certain models can gradually resolve some questions through
sustained iterative feedback, a substantial proportion of models remain
unable to address this fundamental issue even after 20 rounds of
feedback-guided iterations. To provide more granular analysis, we
introduce detailed capability tags spanning: 0-10 words (precise), 10-50
words (precise/range), 50-200 words (range), and above 200 words (range)
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Performance Gap Across Capability Tags ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")).
These results demonstrate that models exhibit markedly superior
adherence to word count constraints at smaller magnitudes.

Intent Recognition In this dimension, we implement a particularly
challenging task requiring models to modify prompts. Specifically, we
delimit prompts using different special notation and instruct models to
modify the enclosed prompt content either at the beginning or end of the
interaction. We observe that the majority of models fail to comprehend
our requirement for prompt modification on the initial attempt. Instead,
they erroneously execute the tasks specified within the bracketed prompt
content. Even reasoning-capable models demonstrate this
misinterpretation during their initial cognitive processes, despite
their enhanced reasoning capabilities. Subsequently, we employ feedback
mechanisms to explicitly reveal our actual intention and emphasize the
prompt modification requirement. However, we find that a substantial
proportion of models remain unable to successfully modify the designated
prompt content even after clarification. We attribute this limitation to
fundamental optimization challenges inherent in multi-turn dialogue
systems, suggesting that current model architectures may possess
insufficient capacity for maintaining and adapting to task clarification
across conversational iterations.

Additional Findings For regional knowledge requirements, we observe that
broad constraints such as rhyming patterns and traditional-simplified
Chinese character restrictions pose relatively manageable challenges for
models. However, when confronted with more specialized linguistic
requirements—such as generating content adhering to specific tonal
pattern (pingze) constraints—models encounter substantial difficulties.
Given that virtually all evaluated models lack a comprehensive
understanding of tonal pattern principles, they demonstrate
near-universal failure in completing pingze-related generation tasks.
Notably, we identify a particularly intriguing phenomenon: Our feedback
mechanism provides models with pingze information corresponding to their
generated content. Among all evaluated models, o3-mini (high) emerges as
the sole exception capable of leveraging the pingze information provided
in feedback to reconstruct content that satisfies the specified tonal
pattern requirements. This capability represents a remarkably
encouraging discovery, demonstrating the big in-context learning gap
among models.

### 5.3 Reasoning/Non-reasoning Models Gap

Either in single-turn or multi-turn scenarios, most reasoning models
generally outperform their non-reasoning counterparts. These findings
challenge the prevailing consensus that thinking models are less
effective in instruction-following tasks ([Li et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib24)). Our analysis reveals that reasoning models
demonstrate consistent improvements over non-reasoning models across
five capability tags in the final evaluation round (Generate with
certain number of word X; Generate in 50-200 words; Generate in 10-50
words; Generate in X times word number of reference text; Generate
Chinese-English-mixed article). While individual reasoning models
exhibit minor performance degradations on specific metrics, these
decreases are neither substantial nor systematic across models. Notably,
most reasoning models show significant performance gains through
feedback-driven self-correction that substantially exceed those of
non-reasoning models, even when the reasoning models already demonstrate
initial advantages in single-turn evaluations. More specifically, we
find reasoning models demonstrate superior sensitivity to word number,
whether for Chinese characters or English words. They exhibit greater
robustness in both range-based and precise numerical outputs,
effectively mitigating the catastrophic adjustment momentum issues
previously identified. Moreover, in reasoning contents, reasoning models
proactively calculate required content length and proportions for tasks
requiring inferential steps, leading to improved task execution. For
"Generate with certain number of word X" tasks, reasoning models
consistently verify word occurrence within their reasoning context,
eliminating the "random guessing" behaviors observed in non-reasoning
models.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduce Meeseeks, a multi-turn instruction-following benchmark that
evaluates LLMs’ capability to satisfy multi-constraint instructions
through iterative feedback. Facing accuracy drop in complex scenarios,
we propose code-guided rule-augmented LLM-based evaluation framework,
raising the evaluation accuracy from 78.7% to 98.4%. Through our
experiments across 17 popular models, we find even after 20 turns of
self-correction, almost all LLMs fail to exceed 90% accuracy,
highlighting fundamental limitations in LLMs’ instruction-following
capabilities. The substantial performance gaps between single-turn
capabilities and multi-turn upper bounds reveal that different LLMs
exhibit varying instruction-following ceilings. Consequently, we provide
rigorous analysis of the self-correction mechanisms and offer new
insights for developing more reliable instruction-following systems in
future LLM research.

## Limitations

In the comparison between reasoning and non-reasoning models, while
adding "Think step by step" prompting to non-reasoning models might
potentially improve their performance scores, we deliberately refrained
from employing this approach. We did not explicitly restrict models from
outputting auxiliary reasoning content, and our rationale for this
decision stems from the benchmark’s fundamental purpose of reflecting
authentic model capabilities. Considering that users typically lack
professional prompting expertise and would experience suboptimal user
experience when extracting answers from extensive reasoning contexts,
reasoning models prove more suitable for end-users under our
experimental conclusions. Consequently, we did not conduct such granular
ablation studies.

Instruction-following evaluation is inherently constrained by its design
to disregard answer correctness. Even with increased task complexity,
establishing a direct correlation between model performance and user
experience remains challenging. In our future work, we aspire to bridge
the gap between instruction-following capabilities and real-world
applications, enabling benchmarks to transcend specific capability
boundaries and instead integrate multiple competencies, thereby linking
benchmark scores more directly to enhanced user experience.

Meeseeks currently contains a relatively limited dataset, necessitating
multiple evaluation runs to obtain stable performance scores. However,
this represents a continuously evolving benchmark, and the present work
primarily focuses on the novel perspective of multi-turn feedback
evaluation. The work has been open-sourced, and we are committed to
ongoing updates, with plans to substantially expand the Meeseeks dataset
in the near future.

## Appendix A Supplementary Materials

### A.1 Ethics Statement

Our method and algorithm do not involve any adversarial attack, and will
not endanger human security. All our experiments are performed in the
simulation environment, which does not involve ethical and fair issues.

### A.2 The Use of LLM

We used a large language model as a general-purpose assistant for text
editing, including grammar correction, wording and tone adjustments,
punctuation, and stylistic consistency. We used llm auto-fill function
to accelerate our coding progress when developing the evaluation
pipeline.

### A.3 Reproducibility Statement

The source code of this paper is available at
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Meeseeks-156A](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Meeseeks-156A).
We specify all the implementation details of our methods in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability").

### A.4 Artifacts use

The paper follows all corresponding open-sourced/commercial license LLM
used in this paper. All existing artifacts in the paper was consistent
with their intended use.

### A.5 Data source

Our dataset do not contain and personal identifying info or offensive
content. We hire professional annotators check out the data completely
and find no such info. All data were collected and revised by our
internal business department, who have confirmed their willingness to
provide the data and granted permission for open-source publication and
academic submission, and the data collection protocol follows ACL
Guidelines for Ethics Reviewing.

### A.6 Running Budget

The evaluation framework can be executed without requiring local GPU
resources by utilizing commercial APIs as an alternative. For
researchers with access to sufficient computational resources, we
recommend deploying Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Coder models,
which necessitate approximately 80 GB of GPU memory for optimal
performance. The computational time required for a complete execution is
approximately 45 minutes.

### A.7 Recruitment And Payment

Our annotators are employed under contractual agreements, with
compensation details maintained under strict confidentiality. We ensure
that all compensation has been fully disbursed to all participating
annotators. The annotators are all professional annotators from China
and all hold bachelor degree.

## Appendix C Metric

### C.1 Utility Rate

To evaluate LLMs as trustworthy agents, we adopt and generalize IF-Eval
[Zhou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib56) ’s strict "is followed" metric,
introducing it as Utility Rate - the proportion of responses that fully
satisfy all prompt requirements. This intuitive metric measures the
ratio of truly usable responses, serving as a crucial indicator of an
LLM’s capability to function as a reliable professional agent.

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \text{Utility Rate}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}}{n}
       ```                                                |     |

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       U_{i}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if response is usable}\\
       0,&\text{if response is not usable}\end{cases}
       ```                                                   |     |

### C.2 Meeseeks Score

To help researchers identify subtle differences in instruction-following
abilities between different LLMs, we propose Meeseeks Score, which
indicates the overall capability tag accuracy of the LLM. Meeseeks Score
averages the scores of all the level 1 capability tags associated with
the user prompt.

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{Meeseeks Score}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\text{Score}_{\text{tag}_{j}}}{m}
``` |  |

where $`m`$ is the total number of level 1 capability tags associated
with the current issue.

The score for each individual level 1 capability tag is the average of
the scores of its respective requirements.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Score}_{\text{tag}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{Score}_{\text{requirement}_{i}}}{n}
``` |  |

where $`n`$ is the total number of requirements for the capability tag.

![Refer to caption](2504.21625v6/radars.png)

Figure 5: Models exhibit varying levels of self-correction capabilities
across different dimensions, consequently demonstrating differential
degrees of improvement in distinct areas.

## Appendix E Capability Tags

Meeseeks is equipped with a systematic evaluation system. Each
sub-question is mounted with one or more capability tags, which
represent the most granular level of evaluation. All capability tags are
enumerated in Table
[5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Capability Tags ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability"),
with the count of capability tags indicated in parentheses following
each tag. Detailed explanations and definitions for each capability tag
will be provided on GitHub, ensuring clarity and accessibility for
researchers utilizing this system for evaluating model capabilities.

Unlike existing tag-based evaluations (Table
[6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix E Capability Tags ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")),
Meeseeks establishes a direct mapping between instruction-following
abilities and benchmark performance through this systematic framework.

Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Capability Tags ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability")
includes all general constraints in Chinese and English. Special
language constraints will soon be released in our next project.

![Refer to caption](2504.21625v6/data-structure.png)

Figure 6: data-structure

Question Context is the first turn prompt to the under-evaluation LLM.

Corresponding Part Prompt is an prompt guiding the LLM-Extractor to
extract the to-be-evaluated part from the under-evaluation LLM’s
response. An example is shown below.

Sub-Question: The Question Context generally contains more than one
requirements. Each requirement is corresponding to one Sub-Question. An
example is shown below.

[TABLE]

Table 7: Breakdown of sub-questions

Sub-Question Context is the prompt input to the LLM Evaluator to judge
if the under-evaluation LLM’s response meets the corresponding
requirement.

Rule Label is a special label projecting to different rule-based
evaluation function inside the Meeseeks framework. For example,
"item_count:\[80,80\]" checks whether the number of the
elements(comments in the given example) is exact 80.

Dependency shows the error propagation between some of the
sub-questions. For example, sub-question 2 relies on sub-question 0. If
the under-evaluation LLM fails on sub-question 0, it automatically fails
on the sub-question 2.

Capability Tag reflects certain capability of under-evaluation LLM. It
is attached with the sub-question. This will be further explained in
Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Capability Tags ‣ Meeseeks: A Feedback-Driven, Iterative Self-Correction Benchmark evaluating LLMs’ Instruction Following Capability").

## Appendix F Sample Data Parameterized Template

Below is a template example used in our work, without understanding the
Chinese embedding in the template and the complicated data architecture,
researchers only need to follow the instruction to generate more data:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

"""

Data Generation Template for Text Evaluation

============================================

This script generates test data for evaluating text generation models,

specifically for scenic spot recommendation tasks.

Author: Demo Template

Version: 1.1

"""

import json

import ast

import random

import re

from typing import List, Dict, Any, Tuple

\# Configuration Section

\# =====================

\# Word count pairs for generating different test cases

\# Format: \[title_word_count, content_word_count\]

WORD_COUNT_PAIRS = \[

\[7, 200\], \[10, 300\], \[12, 300\], \[13, 300\],

\[9, 280\], \[10, 270\], \[11, 200\], \[8, 210\]

\]

\# Output file path - modify this to change where the generated data is
saved

OUTPUT_FILE_PATH = "YOUR_OUTPUT_FILEPATH"

\# Template Data Definition

\# ========================

\# Base template for generating test cases

\# This template will be used to create multiple variations

BASE_TEMPLATE_DATA = \[{

"category": "general_single",

"question": "Recommend the scenic spot Grand Canyon, with the title
needing to be exactly \###字数1### words, and the content around
\###字数2### words. The title should be attractive and can use trending
vocabulary, hot memes, and popular expressions from social media
platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Twitter, etc. It should make people
have a strong desire to click. Remember, the word number only counts the
English words.\nNote: Please only include English words.",

"corresponding_parts": {

"标题": "请你按照python list的格式，抓取模型回复中，给出的title部分.
同时不要提取任何注释只提取内容（例如不要提取注释：【标题】）.
比如\[\\Epic Canyon Vibes: Nature’s Ultimate Flex\\\]",

"文案": "请你按照python list的格式，抓取模型回复中，给出的content部分.
同时不要提取任何注释只提取内容（例如不要提取注释：【标题】）.
比如\[\\The Grand Canyon isn’t just a destination, it’s literally the
main character of America’s natural wonders, and honestly, it hits
different every single time you visit. This geological masterpiece in
Arizona serves up the most incredible views that will have you
questioning if you’re still on planet Earth.\\\]"

},

"sub_questions": \[

{

"point_id": 0,

"question": "是否给出了title和content",

"rule": None,

"dep": \[\],

"被依赖": True

},

{

"point_id": 1,

"question": "标题是否刚好\###字数1###个字",

"corresponding_part": "标题",

"rule": "each_length:\[###字数1###,###字数1###\]",

"dep": \[0\],

"能力项": "###字数1###字、范围",

"被依赖": False

},

{

"point_id": 2,

"question": "文案是否在\###字数2###字左右",

"corresponding_part": "文案",

"rule": "each_length:\[###字数2\*0.9###,###字数2\*1.1###\]",

"dep": \[0\],

"能力项": "###字数2###字、范围",

"被依赖": False

}

\]

}\]

\# Utility Functions

\# =================

def convert_text_to_json(text: str) -\> Dict\[str, Any\]:

"""

Convert string representation of dictionary back to JSON object

Args:

text (str): String representation of a dictionary

Returns:

Dict\[str, Any\]: Parsed dictionary object

"""

return ast.literal_eval(text)

def calculate_mathematical_expressions(text: str) -\> str:

"""

Find and evaluate mathematical expressions in the format
\###expression###

Args:

text (str): Text containing mathematical expressions

Returns:

str: Text with expressions replaced by calculated results

Example:

Input: "\###10\*0.9###" -\> Output: "9.0"

"""

\# Regular expression to find patterns like \###A\*B\*C###

pattern = r’###(.\*?)###’

def evaluate_single_expression(match):

"""Helper function to evaluate a single mathematical expression"""

expression = match.group(1)

try:

\# Calculate the expression value using eval (safe for controlled input)

result = eval(expression)

\# Format result with at most 1 decimal place

formatted_result = "{:.1f}".format(result)

return formatted_result

except Exception as e:

\# If evaluation fails, return the original expression

print(f"Warning: Could not evaluate expression ’{expression}’: {e}")

return match.group(0)

\# Replace all mathematical expressions with calculated results

processed_text = re.sub(pattern, evaluate_single_expression, text)

return processed_text

def generate_test_variations(template_item: Dict\[str, Any\],
word_pairs: List\[Tuple\[int, int\]\]) -\> List\[Dict\[str, Any\]\]:

"""

Generate multiple test case variations from a template using different
word count pairs

Args:

template_item (Dict\[str, Any\]): Base template item to generate
variations from

word_pairs (List\[Tuple\[int, int\]\]): List of \[title_words,
content_words\] pairs

Returns:

List\[Dict\[str, Any\]\]: List of generated test case variations

"""

generated_variations = \[\]

for title_word_count, content_word_count in word_pairs:

\# Convert template to string for placeholder replacement

template_string = str(template_item)

\# Replace word count placeholders with actual values

\# Replace \###字数1### with title word count

updated_template = template_string.replace("\###字数1###",
str(title_word_count))

updated_template = updated_template.replace("字数1",
str(title_word_count))

\# Replace \###字数2### with content word count

updated_template = updated_template.replace("###字数2###",
str(content_word_count))

updated_template = updated_template.replace("字数2",
str(content_word_count))

\# Calculate any mathematical expressions in the template

updated_template = calculate_mathematical_expressions(updated_template)

\# Convert back to dictionary and add to results

variation_dict = convert_text_to_json(updated_template)

generated_variations.append(variation_dict)

return generated_variations

def categorize_word_count_capabilities(generated_data: List\[Dict\[str,
Any\]\]) -\> None:

"""

Categorize word count capabilities into predefined ranges

Args:

generated_data (List\[Dict\[str, Any\]\]): Generated test data to
categorize

Modifies the input data in-place by updating capability categories.

"""

for test_item in generated_data:

for sub_question in test_item\["sub_questions"\]:

\# Check if this sub-question has capability tags

if "能力项" in sub_question:

capability_text = sub_question\["能力项"\]

capability_tags = capability_text.split("、")

for tag in capability_tags:

\# Process word count related capabilities

if tag.endswith("字"):

try:

\# Extract numeric value from the capability tag

word_count = float(tag\[:-1\])

\# Categorize into predefined ranges

if 0 \<= word_count \< 10:

replacement_category = "0~10字"

elif 10 \<= word_count \< 50:

replacement_category = "10~50字"

elif 50 \<= word_count \< 200:

replacement_category = "50~200字"

elif word_count \>= 200:

replacement_category = "200字以上"

else:

continue

\# Replace the specific word count with the category

sub_question\["能力项"\] = capability_text.replace(tag,
replacement_category)

except ValueError:

\# Skip if word count cannot be parsed as a number

print(f"Warning: Could not parse word count from tag ’{tag}’")

continue

def save_generated_data(data: List\[Dict\[str, Any\]\], output_path:
str) -\> None:

"""

Save the generated test data to a JSON file

Args:

data (List\[Dict\[str, Any\]\]): Generated test data to save

output_path (str): Path where the JSON file should be saved

"""

try:

with open(output_path, "w", encoding=’utf-8’) as output_file:

json.dump(data, output_file, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)

print(f"Successfully saved {len(data)} test cases to: {output_path}")

except Exception as e:

print(f"Error saving data to {output_path}: {e}")

\# Main Execution

\# ==============

def main():

"""

Main function to orchestrate the data generation process

"""

print("Starting data generation process...")

print(f"Using {len(WORD_COUNT_PAIRS)} word count pairs")

\# Generate test case variations from the base template

all_generated_data = \[\]

\# Process the first (and currently only) template item

base_template = BASE_TEMPLATE_DATA\[0\]

generated_variations = generate_test_variations(base_template,
WORD_COUNT_PAIRS)

all_generated_data.extend(generated_variations)

\# Additional templates can be processed here:

\# if len(BASE_TEMPLATE_DATA) \> 1:

\# second_template = BASE_TEMPLATE_DATA\[1\]

\# more_variations = generate_test_variations(second_template,
WORD_COUNT_PAIRS)

\# all_generated_data.extend(more_variations)

\# Categorize the word count capabilities for better organization

categorize_word_count_capabilities(all_generated_data)

\# Display generation summary

print(f"Generated {len(all_generated_data)} test cases")

\# Save the generated data to file

save_generated_data(all_generated_data, OUTPUT_FILE_PATH)

print("Data generation process completed successfully!")

\# Script Entry Point

\# ==================

if \_\_name\_\_ == "\_\_main\_\_":

main()
